description: Final year CS student leading this team into NASA Space Apps  our strength is storytelling and design, and we're tackling the health conditions in space missions . Looking for someone strong in coding/dev to match that creative side, bonus if you know geospatial or data, please join us if you want to build something that actually looks and feels polished, not a bare minimum demo.
summary: AfterDust is an animated short film and website about the machines left behind by NASA. The film follows Opportunity, the Mars rover, waking up on its last day (2018). As a dust storm rolls in, it reminisces about the machines that came before it. These include Viking 1, the first functioning U.S. lander on Mars, and the Eagle from Apollo 11, still sitting on the Moon today. The film ends as Perseverance, a new rover, arrives. This is fictional however all the machines, dates and locations are real. The website allows the film to be turned into a timeline of 16 of the machines on NASA’s list. These range from Surveyor 3 (1967) to Ingenuity (2024). Each has a real photo from NASA, a short story, their last words (if any) and a narrator. This is aimed at space fans of school age, to give them an emotional experience before showing them what science they enabled.
details:
Overview

AfterDust is made up of two parts. The first part is a 3 minute short film. It details Opportunity’s final day on Mars, as they reflect on the past machines Viking 1 and Apollo 11’s Eagle. Opportunity’s mission comes to an end due to a global dust storm and Perseverance arrives in Jezero Crater. The second part is a website containing the short film and a timeline of 16 machines NASA have left on the Moon, Mars and deep space.

Implementation

Our team wrote the storyline, script and dialogue. The 3D scenes were created and animated in Blender using NASA’s free 3D models of the rovers and landers. The scenes were rendered using the EEVEE engine. Flashbacks were created using real photos and launch videos from NASA’s Image and Video Library. The voices were created synthetically using the open source Kokoro text-to-speech model and were altered to give a robotic sound. The music and sound effects were created using code. The website consists of one static page, hosted on Vercel. The background is a starfield, and contains the film, glowing points on the timeline and a voice over saying ‘Hear more about it’.

Benefits

Most people will know the names and dates of these machines. By giving Opportunity a voice and showing their final day, young viewers will care more. The website then provides them with all the facts and links to more information. All the machines have links to their page on NASA.

Creativity

The short film shows the perspective of the machine. Opportunity reflects on past machines and waits for their successor. Real hardware is used within a fictional storyline. This is clearly stated in the credits.

Considerations

All dates, locations and facts were accurate to NASA. We clearly stated what was fictional. No NASA logos were used in any generated content. No copyrighted music was used and all AI generated content was labelled.

Tools Used

Blender, Python (NumPy, SciPy, Pillow), FFmpeg, Kokoro text-to-speech model, Canva, HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Vercel, Claude (Anthropic)
